newsitem.title: CHINA: China to curb exodus of rural workers to cities.
newsitem.headline: China to curb exodus of rural workers to cities.

text.p: China plans to curb the exodus of surplus rural workers looking for jobs in cities by developing small towns and creating jobs for them there, the China Daily said on Monday.
The Ministry of Construction envisages relocating 30 million surplus farm workers to small towns across the country by 2000, the newspaper said.
Vice-Minister of Construction Mao Rubai was quoted as saying the project would target the building of public facilities in science, education, culture and health. He did not give a figure.
About 150,000 public toilets and 1,700 parks have been built in rural townships, the newspaper said.

The population of China's 50,000 small towns was expected to surge to 200 million by the turn of the century, the newspaper said without giving a comparative figure. Of the existing towns, the government would prioritise the development of 10,000.
About 3,000 of the towns would have a population of between 20,000 and 30,000 each by 2000, while another 7,000 would have more than 10,000 residents each, it said.
Large-scale construction of residential housing, public facilities and other building projects would improve living conditions in those towns, the newspaper said.
About one million rural enterprises, employing more than 150 million people, have been set up in the 50,000 small towns.

The small towns attracted 60 million people in rural surplus labour between 1991 and 1995. Migrant workers have flooded China's major cities over the last 10 years, with the easing of restrictions on movements from rural to urban areas.
China has an estimated 80 million migrant workers, of who 20 million work in provinces other than their own.
Migrant workers are allowed to live in cities but do not have the right of permanent residence. Many live in crowded makeshift buildings close to their place of work.

Some economists argue that the labour migration is of great economic benefit, channelling money from the cities to rural areas, meeting urban labour shortages and raising the skills and knowledge of the labourers.
But long-term urban residents blame the migrants for rising crime and drug abuse. They also say these workers disregard sanitation and tight family planning rules by having more than one child.
